title: the mouth full of universe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mouth full of universe: Yashoda looked for dirt and saw everything, her own village and herself inside it. What small thing turned out bigger than you expected? Day eight hundred ninety-one.
screen: `THE MOUTH FULL OF UNIVERSE.` · `SHE SAW HERSELF INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: It wasn't the first time. A chapter earlier, the Bhagavata tells a smaller version. Yashoda is nursing her baby, and he yawns, the way babies do. And in that yawn, for an instant, she sees the sky, the earth, the stars, the oceans, mountains and forests. She trembles and shuts her eyes. Then the moment passes and he's just a yawning baby again. So yesterday's vision was not her first. And that raises the question for today: after you've seen something like that, what happens to the next ordinary morning?
screen: `A YAWN WHILE NURSING.` → `SKY, EARTH, STARS, FOR AN INSTANT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: Back in the yard, Yashoda is still standing over her son, bewildered, bowing inwardly to whatever this is. And then the text says something startling. Krishna spreads his maya over her, his power to veil, and it takes the form of a mother's love for her son. And she forgets. The vision is gone. She picks him up, sets him on her lap, and her heart is full of affection for him, just as it was before. The very next thing we hear is that she's his mother again, as if nothing happened. Notice what the story chooses. It could have ended with Yashoda as a great sage, transformed forever, seeing God in her child every waking moment. Instead the vision is taken back, on purpose, and what replaces it is love. The Bhagavata treats that love as no small thing. King Parikshit, listening to the story, asks the sage telling it: what did Nanda and Yashoda ever do, to be given a love like this? And the sage answers with a story about a former life, in which they asked for one thing: supreme devotion to the Lord, once they were born on earth. In this telling, being his parents is how that wish is granted. So the forgetting isn't a loss in this telling. It's the gift working. Some devotional schools hold up Yashoda's love, a parent's love, as a very sweet way of loving God: not bowing to the infinite from far away, but feeding him, scolding him, holding him. She has seen what he is. And she is allowed to keep loving who he is to her.
screen: `THE YAWN CAME FIRST.` · `A VEIL SHAPED LIKE A MOTHER'S LOVE.` · `SHE FORGETS, AND HOLDS HIM.` · then, large: `THE FORGETTING IS THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breath slow on its own. Bring to mind someone very ordinary to you, someone you see so often you've stopped really looking: a partner, a child, a parent, a roommate, a coworker. For a few breaths, let them be enormous: a whole life, a whole world inside them that you'll never fully see. Then let that go, and simply picture their everyday face, and let warmth come back to it. Both are true. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer as the bell rings. The bell holds the time.
The mouth full of universe. A mother who saw everything in her son, and was given the grace to forget it and simply love him.
screen: `THE MOUTH FULL OF UNIVERSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the mouth full of universe. Today, with one familiar person, set aside what you know about them and simply enjoy their company. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: In some Krishna traditions, devotees relate to Krishna as Yashoda and Nanda do, as a beloved child, caring for small images of the infant Krishna with food, clothing and lullabies.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the whole universe inside your little boy's mouth. what happens next?
options: you bow to him and never treat him as a child again.
you forget it, and take him on your lap with love.
you run to tell the whole village.
fork.reveal: Krishna veils the vision with a mother's love, and she forgets and holds him. the text treats the forgetting as a gift.

original.note: Sanskrit: maya, the veiling power; here it takes the form of a mother's love.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yashoda forgets because the vision was too much.
what it means: Krishna veils it himself, and the veil he uses is her own love for him.
what a scholar hears: the text answers why with a former life, in which Nanda and Yashoda, then Drona and Dhara, asked for supreme devotion to the Lord.
